conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. You're in the hospital because you had chest pain while in the ER. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been drinking a lot—like, several quarts of vodka and beer—plus using cocaine and heroin for about five days. I was under a bridge. Then my chest started hurting, real sharp in the center, didn’t go away with the nitro spray I sometimes use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for sharing. Your alcohol level was quite high when you arrived—355—and your urine test showed opioids but no cocaine. The chest pain wasn’t from a heart attack—we checked your troponins twice and they were normal, and your EKG didn’t show new changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? But I’ve had stents before—four of them. I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You do have serious heart disease, and the EKG still shows old damage from a past heart attack. But this episode doesn’t look like a new one. The pain might be from withdrawing from alcohol and heroin. You mentioned tremors and diarrhea—those are withdrawal signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been shaking bad. Haven’t had a drink or anything since yesterday. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. That’s why we started you on a medication called Valium every few hours—it helps with withdrawal and prevents seizures. We’re also watching your blood pressure and heart rate, which are a bit high—154 over 111, heart rate 106.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t take my blood pressure pills lately. I lost them. But I take lisinopril and metoprolol usually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted your lisinopril. But we’re holding the metoprolol for now—because of the recent cocaine use, it could be risky. We’ll talk to your primary doctor about restarting it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We repeated your blood work, including another troponin—it’s still negative. Your CK level was a bit high, but that’s likely from muscle strain or dehydration, not heart damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay to go? I feel shaky but no chest pain now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Medically, you’re stable, but you’re still in withdrawal. Leaving now carries risks—like seizures, heart issues, or even death. We’d really prefer you stay for full detox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I need to get out. I’ve been here before. Can I at least get some help for rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, social work spoke with you and gave info on two rehab programs—both might have openings tomorrow. Please call them. We also started a new medication—Imdur, a long-acting nitrate—to help with blood pressure and possible angina.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m stopping metoprolol and starting Imdur? What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep your aspirin, Plavix, pravastatin, lisinopril, citalopram, and clonazepam. The oxycodone at night is still okay. But no more cocaine—mixing it with metoprolol is dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’ve decided to leave against medical advice. I want to make sure you understand: withdrawal symptoms can get worse, and your heart is already weak. Please call your primary doctor and those rehab centers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I’ll make the calls tomorrow. I don’t want to keep doing this—it’s killing me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good step. We’re giving you a list of your meds and instructions. If chest pain returns, or you feel confused or have a seizure, go back to the ER immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for not giving up on me, even though I’m leaving early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We care about your health. Please take care of yourself. You’re strong enough to make a change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I really will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your stool was black and green. That could be from something you ate, but if it stays dark or you feel weak, get it checked. Could be stomach bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate some weird food under the bridge. I’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fair enough. Just be careful. Here’s your medication list and contact numbers. Please call someone tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m heading out now. I’ll call the rehab place first thing.
